WHO is not liable for any damages arising from the use of its materials. The WHO Patient Safety Programme has been instrumental in raising global awareness of patient safety concepts and strategies. It has secured high-level commitments from health ministers and leaders in WHO Member States, provided evidence-based guidance and tools, and championed the voices of patients and families affected by unsafe care. The program has evolved, requiring new priorities and directions to address the changing global context of patient safety. Unsafe medication practices and errors are a leading cause of avoidable harm in healthcare systems worldwide. The scale and nature of this harm vary between low-, middle-, and high-income countries. Globally, medication errors are estimated to cost $42 billion annually. Patients in low-income countries experience twice as many disability-adjusted life years lost due to medication-related harm compared to those in high-income countries. Errors often occur due to weak medication systems and human factors such as fatigue, poor environmental conditions, or staff shortages, leading to severe harm, disability, or death. Errors are most frequent during medication administration but can occur at any stage of the process. The third Global Patient Safety Challenge, Medication Without Harm, aims to reduce severe, avoidable medication-related harm by 50% over five years. This will be achieved by addressing weaknesses in healthcare systems and improving practices at all stages of the medication process, including prescribing, dispensing, administering, monitoring, and use. The challenge emphasizes the importance of strengthening systems and practices to initiate corrective actions within countries, ultimately improving patient safety and reducing harm. The challenge's strategic framework focuses on four key domains: patients and the public, medicines, healthcare professionals, and systems and practices of medication. Actions are categorized into early priority actions, developmental programs, and global initiatives. Early actions include managing high-risk situations, polypharmacy, and care transitions. Developmental programs involve convening experts, healthcare professionals, stakeholders, and patient representatives to design targeted safety improvement programs. Global initiatives aim to provide guidance, strengthen human resource capacity, improve data quality, promote research, and engage regulatory agencies and international actors to enhance medication safety. The challenge also highlights the importance of empowering patients to safely manage their medications and addressing issues such as confusing medication names, labeling, and packaging. Healthcare professionals must prescribe and administer medicines in ways that minimize harm, and systems must be designed to be resilient to risks and errors. The WHO's efforts in medication safety are driven by the need to save lives and reduce avoidable harm. The organization seeks to foster global commitment and action to improve medication safety, ensuring that patient safety remains a core component of universal health coverage.
